titre: Fountain, the Urinal That Was Never Exhibited
accroche: The most debated work of the 20th century was never shown to the public, and its author may not be who you think.
contenu_vulgarise:
In April 1917, the Society of Independent Artists holds its first exhibition in New York, with a simple rule: no jury, and any artist who pays the entry fee has his or her work shown. Among the submissions arrives a porcelain urinal, bought at a plumbing supply store, placed upside down and signed “R. Mutt.” It is titled *Fountain*.

The committee, embarrassed, does not formally reject it; the rules don't allow that. It simply never places it in the exhibition hall. The work disappears behind a partition, no one sees it, and its signatory, R. Mutt, cannot be found in the society's registers.

## The Gesture

A few days later, the photographer Alfred Stieglitz photographs the urinal in his studio. The picture appears in *The Blind Man*, a New York magazine close to the Dada movement, accompanied by an unsigned text that will become one of the most quoted sentences of modern art: whether Mr. Mutt made the fountain with his own hands or not has no importance; he chose it.

That sentence sums up on its own what is at stake in the object. A mass-produced urinal, removed from its function, turned over, signed with a pseudonym, ceases to be a urinal without any hand having sculpted anything. What makes the work is no longer the execution, but the decision to designate an object as such. The original of *Fountain* is lost shortly after the aborted exhibition. What we see in museums today are sixteen replicas commissioned between the 1950s and 1960s, approved by the signatory of the original gesture.

## What It Shifts

Who, exactly, signed R. Mutt? The long-accepted version attributes the gesture to Marcel Duchamp, who would himself allude to it in his writings. But more recent research, notably that of the art historian Glyn Thompson, a former professor at the University of Leeds, points to another lead: the handwriting on the urinal would match that of the German artist Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven, then living in Philadelphia, the city where the urinal is said to have been manufactured by a local plumber, a city Duchamp himself never visited.

The hypothesis remains debated, without settling the question definitively. But it adds, to a work already built on the idea that the gesture of designating matters more than the hand that executes, one more doubt about the hand that, precisely, did the designating.

carte.punch: Fountain, the urinal sent to a jury-free exhibition, was never shown to the public.
carte.idee: In 1917, a urinal signed “R. Mutt” and titled Fountain is sent to an exhibition with no jury. The committee does not officially reject it: it simply never places it in the hall. A magazine publishes its photograph, and the original disappears shortly afterward.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full context of the Society of Independent Artists and the afterlife of the work.

quiz.question: What exactly does the committee of the Society of Independent Artists do about the urinal signed “R. Mutt” in 1917?
choix: It formally votes to exclude it despite the announced no-selection rule
It displays it in a separate room reserved for controversial works
It never officially rejects it but never places it in the exhibition hall
It accepts it and displays it normally, before removing it under pressure from the public
quiz.explication: The rules of the society, which used no jury, required accepting any work by an artist who had paid the entry fee. The committee therefore never formally rejected it: it simply set it aside, outside the exhibition hall, which amounts in practice to sidelining it without owning the decision.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the famous sentence, published unsigned in The Blind Man, say about Fountain?
choix: That Mr. Mutt will remain anonymous forever, and that the work belongs to no one
That the Society of Independent Artists was wrong not to exhibit such a daring work
That whether Mr. Mutt made the fountain with his own hands or not has no importance; he chose it
That modern art no longer needs any physical object to exist
quiz_supplementaire.explication: This sentence sums up what is at stake in the work: what makes it exist is no longer manual execution, but the decision to designate an object as such, regardless of who made it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do we see in museums today under the name Fountain?
choix: Sixteen replicas commissioned between the 1950s and 1960s, approved by the signatory of the original gesture
The original urinal of 1917, restored and kept at the Philadelphia Museum of Art
A digital reconstruction, the original and all the replicas having been destroyed
A single replica, commissioned by Marcel Duchamp himself just before his death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The original of Fountain is lost shortly after the aborted exhibition of 1917; what we see in museums are sixteen replicas commissioned in the 1950s and 1960s, approved by the signatory of the gesture.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Glyn Thompson's hypothesis attributing Fountain to Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven rest on?
choix: A signed letter from Freytag-Loringhoven, found in Duchamp's archives
The direct testimony of Alfred Stieglitz, who supposedly saw Freytag-Loringhoven drop off the object
A stylistic comparison between Fountain and other works signed by Freytag-Loringhoven
The handwriting on the urinal and its manufacture in Philadelphia, a city Duchamp never visited
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Thompson relies on a handwriting match between the signature on the urinal and that of Freytag-Loringhoven, and on its manufacture in Philadelphia, a city where Duchamp never set foot.
